strengths: Identifies an important and previously underexplored failure mode: existing unlearning methods suppress the model's ability to use forgotten knowledge when it is re-supplied in context (Contextual QA). This is a novel and practically relevant evaluation dimension, well-motivated by RAG deployments.

The empirical diagnosis is systematic: six unlearning methods across two instruction-tuned LLMs (Gemma-2B-IT, Qwen3-8B), three forget ratios (1%, 5%, 10%), with both ROUGE-L and an LLM-judge metric, epoch-level training curves, an informative case study (Table 1), and a retrain baseline in the appendix.

The proposed fix is simple, modular, and well-executed: a KL-consistency term against the frozen original model on context-conditioned forget examples, shown to plug into RMU, NPO, and UNDIAL with large gains (e.g., RMU contextual LLM-Judge from <=0.05 to ~0.97-0.99) while preserving Direct QA forgetting and model utility.

Good ablation coverage: forget-ratio ablation (Fig. 4), robustness to paraphrased/reasoning context variants (Table 4), lambda_c sensitivity analysis (Fig. 9), and an explicit discussion of why existing objectives cause contextual suppression (Appendix A.3).
Reproducibility is reasonable: training hyperparameters, prompt templates, judge template, and convergence/lambda selection rules are all documented.
weaknesses: Evaluation scope is narrow for the strength of the claims. All experiments use TOFU (fictitious author profiles); no real-world unlearning benchmarks (e.g., WMDP, MUSE) or actual RAG pipelines are tested. Claims that contextual utility is 'a critical factor for real-world deployment' and that the method is 'general' are therefore only indirectly supported.

The solution is essentially a KL-to-reference regularizer on context-augmented forget data—conceptually straightforward. There is no comparison against obvious baselines, such as simply mixing the contextual SFT examples into the retain term, or other regularization forms, so the specific design is not validated as necessary.

A significant security tension is underexplored: prior work cited by the paper (Hu et al., 2025; Shumailov et al., 2024) shows unlearned knowledge can be resurfaced via contextual cues. The proposed method explicitly preserves/reinforces the model's ability to use forget-set content given context, which plausibly increases susceptibility to elicitation attacks, yet no attack/extractability evaluation (e.g., partial-context prompts, paraphrase attacks on the forget set without full answers) is provided.

Metric reliability concerns: the headline Contextual QA numbers rely on a binary Claude 3.5 Sonnet judge with no human validation or agreement analysis; results are also single-run with no seeds/variance reported, so small deltas (e.g., 2-4 point changes in Direct QA/Utility) cannot be assessed statistically.

Potential selection bias: results are reported at a 'convergence epoch' chosen post hoc and lambda_c is grid-searched selecting the best Contextual QA subject to a tolerance (delta = 0.06) on the vanilla forgetting score, which slightly favors the proposed method; no validation/test split is described.
Presentation has minor polish issues (e.g., 'eaisly intergrate', 'direclty', inconsistent model naming 'Qwen-3-8B'/'Qwen3-8B'), and Figure 2/4 plots are dense and hard to read at print resolution.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuinely underexplored failure mode of LLM unlearning: existing methods that successfully suppress direct recall can still corrupt the model's ability to use the same information when it is supplied in context ('contextual utility'). This is a relevant observation for RAG-style deployments and is orthogonal to prior prompt-based unlearning studies.

The empirical study is reasonably systematic: six unlearning methods, two instruction-tuned models (Gemma-2B-IT, Qwen3-8B), three forget-set ratios, multiple metrics (ROUGE-L, LLM-judge, model utility), with epoch-level training curves in Figures 2, 4, 7-9.

The proposed fix is a simple, modular KL-consistency term that plugs into existing unlearning objectives (NPO, RMU, UNDIAL), and the ablation on lambda_c (Figure 9, Appendix A.4) shows the approach is fairly insensitive to the hyperparameter, which supports practical usability.

The qualitative analyses are informative: case studies (Tables 1, 3, 4) show concrete failure modes (gibberish, hallucination) and the robustness probe with paraphrased/reasoning-required contexts (Section 6.2) goes beyond verbatim-context evaluation.
weaknesses: Conceptual tension with the goal of unlearning is not addressed. The proposed KL term anchors the unlearned model's contextual distribution to the original model, effectively teaching it to fully exploit forgotten knowledge whenever it appears in context. For the core motivating scenarios of unlearning (privacy, right-to-be-forgotten, harmful content removal), a model that retains near-full ability to use the knowledge given a short contextual cue is barely 'unlearned' - this arguably makes the unlearning largely superficial. The paper never discusses whether preserving contextual utility undermines the threat model that motivates unlearning in the first place, nor when contextual preservation is appropriate (e.g., outdated regulations) versus dangerous (e.g., personal data).

Evaluation is confined to the TOFU benchmark of fictitious author profiles - a benign, synthetic setting. No experiments on privacy- or safety-relevant benchmarks (e.g., WMDP, MUSE, even though both are cited), so the claim of ensuring 'responsible and compliant model responses' is not actually tested. Forgetting is also measured only via Direct QA answers; no probing, extraction, or relearning attacks, so residual knowledge is not characterized.

Evidence of test-set-driven selection: the 'convergence epoch' is defined post-hoc as the earliest epoch reaching the global best in Direct QA, Contextual QA, and utility (Appendix A.4), and lambda_c is grid-searched choosing the configuration with the highest Contextual QA score subject to a tolerance (delta=0.06) on the vanilla Direct QA score. Both procedures select on the very metrics reported in Table 2, without held-out validation, multiple seeds, or variance/significance reporting, which inflates the apparent gains of the proposed method relative to vanilla baselines.

The Contextual QA task itself is quite easy: the ground-truth answer is provided verbatim in the prompt, so high scores may largely measure copying rather than genuine contextual grounding. The paper dismisses probability-based metrics but does not report human evaluation, and the LLM-judge (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) is binary and unvalidated against human judgments.

The mechanistic explanation in Appendix A.3 (forget terms 'corrupting' token representations that then impair contextual use) is asserted rather than substantiated by any representation-level analysis; Section 4's framing of why the KL term 'fixes' suppression is likewise informal.

Limited scope of the solution's evaluation: context-aware variants are tested for only three of the six methods, the forget-ratio ablation (Section 6.1) covers only Gemma-2B-IT, and the robustness study (Section 6.2) uses a single method and a single example. No limitations section is provided, and there is no discussion of the ethical implications of weakening unlearning guarantees.

Presentation issues: several typos ('eaisly intergrate', 'direclty'), a mis-attribution of the model-utility metric to Touvron et al. (2023) instead of the TOFU paper, and marginal-evaluable figures where curves are hard to distinguish.

strengths: Identifies and formalizes a genuinely overlooked evaluation dimension—'contextual utility' (whether an unlearned model can still use forgotten knowledge when it is re-supplied in the prompt)—which is highly relevant to real deployments, especially RAG pipelines.

The empirical finding is systematic and convincing: six unlearning methods across two models (Gemma-2B-IT, Qwen3-8B) and three forget ratios consistently degrade Contextual QA (e.g., RMU drops to ~0.00 LLM-Judge even though the gold answer is in the context), supported by quantitative plots (Figs. 2, 8), qualitative case studies (Tables 1, 3, 5), and robustness probes with paraphrased and reasoning-required contexts (Table 4).

The proposed fix is simple, modular, and well-motivated: a KL-consistency term anchoring contextual distributions to the frozen original model, plugged into three representative methods (NPO, RMU, UNDIAL), yielding large gains (e.g., RMU 0.00→0.99 on Gemma) with only marginal changes to Direct QA forgetting and model utility (Table 2).

Good transparency on methodology: prompt and LLM-judge templates are provided (Figs. 5–6), the λc grid search and a principled convergence criterion are described (Appendix A.4), and the λc ablation suggests the method is not brittle to hyperparameter choice.

The analysis in Appendix A.3 offers a plausible mechanistic account of why forget terms (gradient ascent, NPO's probability suppression, RMU's activation perturbation) leak into contextual conditioning.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single benchmark (TOFU, fictitious authors). The cited WMDP and MUSE settings—and real-world sensitive/outdated knowledge more broadly—are untested, so generalization of both the problem finding and the fix beyond synthetic author profiles remains unverified. Notably, on real safety-motivated unlearning targets, deliberately preserving the ability to use forgotten facts given context may conflict with the very goals of unlearning (e.g., a user could paste the removed content and recover the behavior), an ethical tension the paper does not discuss; there is no explicit limitations or ethics section.

The evaluation relies heavily on a binary LLM-Judge (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) and ROUGE-L. In the Contextual QA setting the gold answer appears verbatim in the prompt, so ROUGE-L gains may partly reflect copying rather than genuine grounding, and the judge's reliability is not validated against human annotations. No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported.

A key ablation is missing: comparing the KL anchor against simply fine-tuning on the contextual (q, c, a) examples with a standard cross-entropy loss. Without this, it is unclear how much of the benefit comes from the KL-to-original-model design versus just adding contextual training data.

Some result-selection choices invite scrutiny: 'earliest converged epoch' with a tolerance, and λc selected per method/model via grid search with a 0.06 slack on forgetting effectiveness (Appendix A.4). Although the ablation claims insensitivity, the main-table numbers are best-case selections rather than default settings.

The KL term requires access to the frozen original model, and tuning adds cost for practitioners; the paper mentions but does not quantify the added training overhead or wall-clock cost relative to vanilla unlearning.

Writing contains minor errors (e.g., 'eaisly intergrate', 'direclty') and the framing that contextual utility is a strictly desirable property would benefit from a more careful discussion of when it is not (adversarial or compliance scenarios).

strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes a genuinely overlooked evaluation dimension for LLM unlearning—'contextual utility'—and provides a systematic study showing that six state-of-the-art unlearning methods degrade this capability across two models, three forget ratios, and two benchmarks (TOFU, PISTOL). This is a novel and practically relevant observation.

The proposed fix is a simple, modular KL-consistency term anchored to the frozen pre-unlearning model on (question, context) pairs. It integrates into multiple unlearning objectives (RMU, NPO, UNDIAL, plus DPO, GradDiff, PDU, SimNPO in Appendix A.8) and consistently restores Contextual QA performance (e.g., RMU LLM-Judge from ~0.00 to ~0.99) with small, quantified effects on forgetting and utility (Table 2).

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: human-agreement validation of the LLM-judge (agreement 0.975, Cohen's κ 0.949, Appendix A.2), additional metrics (token accuracy, ChrF, Appendix A.7), a λc sensitivity ablation (Appendix A.6), robustness to paraphrased/reasoning-style contexts (Section 6.2, Table 4), noisy long contexts (Appendix A.10), and conflicting distractors (Appendix A.11).

Mechanistic explanation for why forget terms (GradDiff, NPO, RMU) leak into contextual behavior is provided in Appendix A.5, and qualitative case studies (Tables 1, 3, 4, 6) make failure modes concrete and interpretable.
Honest limitations section acknowledging trade-offs (stronger contextual preservation may slightly weaken Direct QA forgetting), benchmark/model-scale restrictions, and lack of theoretical analysis.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is modest: the context term is essentially a standard KL anchor to the reference model, a well-known regularizer from RLHF/DPO-style setups. The main novelty lies in the evaluation insight rather than the method, which limits methodological originality.

Empirical scope is narrow for a main-track claim of generality: only TOFU (fictitious authors) and PISTOL, models up to 8B, and a single 5%-forget-set main configuration with selected convergence-epoch reporting. Real-world RAG/unlearning scenarios (multi-document, long-context, larger models) are deferred to future work.

Selection methodology raises some concern: λc is chosen via grid search with a convergence criterion that jointly requires Contextual QA and utility to be near their best values, and vanilla baselines are reported at 'converged' epochs—this epoch-selection protocol could favor the proposed method, and per-epoch variability in Figure 2 (e.g., utility oscillations for GradDiff) is not statistically characterized (no seeds/variance).

Some improvements are small where the baseline was already strong (e.g., UNDIAL on Qwen3-8B: 0.97 → 0.98 LLM-Judge), so the 'consistent, large gains' claim overstates results for part of the method set.

The 'why this fixes contextual suppression' analysis (Section 4.1, Appendix A.5) remains informal and narrative; no direct evidence (e.g., probing activation similarity to the original model) is provided to substantiate the representation-corruption hypothesis.

No released-code or artifact statement is evident in the manuscript, which—given the dependence on a specific Claude-3.5-Sonnet judge, templates, and epoch-selection protocol—reduces reproducibility confidence.

The benign-content scoping is appropriate and the impact statement is reasonable, but the paper could more explicitly discuss the tension between restoring contextual utility and removal guarantees in adversarial settings (e.g., WMDP-style hazards), where a user-supplied context could be used to re-activate suppressed knowledge.

strengths: The paper identifies and empirically demonstrates a genuinely underexplored failure mode of LLM unlearning: degradation of 'contextual utility' (the ability to use removed knowledge when it is re-supplied in the prompt). The finding is clearly framed relative to Direct QA evaluations used in prior work, and the distinction from prompt-based unlearning and 'reverse unlearning' work (Shumailov et al., Cooper et al., Hu et al.) is articulated.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this line of work: six unlearning methods across two instruction-tuned models (Gemma-2B-IT, Qwen3-8B), two benchmarks (TOFU and the more realistic, structurally entangled PISTOL), three forget ratios (1/5/10%), additional metrics (token accuracy, ChrF), additional baselines (DPO, GradDiff, PDU, SimNPO), and robustness analyses over paraphrased, noisy, and distractor-laden contexts.

The proposed fix is a simple, plug-in KL-consistency term anchored to the frozen pre-unlearning model on contextualized forget inputs. It integrates into three representative methods (RMU, NPO, UNDIAL) with large gains (e.g., RMU contextual LLM-Judge from ~0.00 to ~0.99 on Gemma) while Direct QA forgetting and model utility shift only marginally.

The LLM-Judge metric is validated against human annotation (agreement 0.975, Cohen's kappa 0.949, bootstrap CIs), and the limitations section honestly discusses the forgetting–contextual-utility trade-off and the scale/scope constraints.

The qualitative analysis of why penalty-based objectives (gradient ascent, NPO, RMU) corrupt representations for contextual use (Appendix A.5) provides useful intuition connecting the observed degradation to specific objective designs.
weaknesses: The methodological contribution is incremental. The context term is essentially standard KL regularization to a frozen reference model on an additional data split — the same design pattern as retain terms in GradDiff and the KL anchors in DPO/RLHF. The novelty lies mostly in recognizing which data split to regularize on, which is a fairly obvious step once the contextual-utility failure mode is identified.

The mechanism analysis is qualitative and hand-wavy. Section 4.1 and Appendix A.5 argue that forget-term penalties 'ripple through the representation space' and corrupt contextual conditioning, but there is no direct evidence (e.g., representation-similarity measurements, activation analyses, or intervention experiments) supporting this causal story. The paper would be substantially stronger with such evidence.

There is a real tension the paper does not fully resolve: the context term trains the model to output the forgotten ground-truth answer (the desired response in Figure 3 contains the protected content) when context is supplied. This is close to re-teaching the forget set in a contextualized format. Direct QA scores remain low, but the paper offers no analysis of whether the removed knowledge has been partially re-internalized (e.g., via probing, membership-inference-style, or extraction attacks) — an important omission given the paper's own privacy/GDPR framing.

The benchmark scope limits external validity. TOFU uses fictitious authors deliberately unseen in pretraining, and both benchmarks are synthetic QA settings; all models are ≤8B. The claim that this matters for real GDPR/copyright deployments (real data, larger models, long-context RAG) remains unverified, and the 'benign but protected content' reframing weakens the original privacy motivation.

Hyperparameter and checkpoint selection use the evaluation metrics themselves: λ_c is chosen by grid search maximizing Contextual LLM-Judge subject to a forgetting tolerance (δ=0.06 chosen by the authors), and the reported epoch is picked by a convergence rule over all three eval metrics. This introduces a mild test-set selection concern; an independent validation split would be more rigorous.

The robustness study in Section 6.2 (Table 4) relies on a single illustrative example and hand-crafted context variants; while Appendix A.10–A.11 provide full-set noisy/distractor evaluations, the headline 'robust to paraphrase and reasoning' claim rests on thin qualitative evidence.

Some reported forgetting degradations are non-trivial and somewhat buried: e.g., NPO Direct QA ROUGE-L rises from 0.31 to 0.36 and LLM-Judge from 0.19 to 0.25 on Gemma (Table 2), and the limitations concede trade-offs. Given that forgetting strength is the primary purpose of unlearning, this deserves more prominence and analysis than it receives.

strengths: Identifies a genuinely important and previously underexplored evaluation dimension: whether unlearning damages the model's ability to use forgotten content when it is legitimately re-supplied as context (e.g., in RAG). The Contextual QA protocol is a sensible, clearly motivated complement to Direct QA.

The empirical study is unusually thorough: six unlearning methods (plus DPO, GradDiff, PDU, SimNPO in the appendix), two model families (Gemma-2B-IT, Qwen3-8B), three forget ratios, two benchmarks (TOFU and the structurally entangled PISTOL), plus robustness probes with paraphrased, noisy, and conflicting contexts.

The proposed fix is simple and modular: a KL-consistency term against the frozen original model on contextual queries, which plugs into existing unlearning objectives. Results are consistent and large (e.g., RMU contextual LLM-Judge from ~0.00 to ~0.99 on Gemma) with marginal changes to Direct QA and utility.

Methodological care: LLM-Judge is validated against human annotation (agreement 0.975, Cohen's kappa 0.949), additional metrics (token accuracy, ChrF) corroborate the main results, and the lambda_c ablation shows the method is insensitive to the key hyperparameter.
Limitations and impact are discussed honestly, including the trade-off between forgetting strength and contextual utility and the constrained model scale.
weaknesses: A tension at the heart of the approach is not fully resolved: the context term anchors the unlearned model's distribution to the original model on inputs containing the forgotten content, so the capability to process this content is deliberately retained. This weakens the unlearning guarantee by construction. Given known relearning/reverse-unlearning attacks (Shumailov et al., 2024; Cooper et al., 2025), an analysis of whether the residual capability enables knowledge recovery (e.g., progressive hinting, jailbreak-style elicitation without verbatim context) would substantially strengthen the claim that forgetting is preserved.

Model selection raises a mild test-set contamination concern: convergence epochs and lambda_c are chosen by jointly optimizing evaluation metrics (Contextual LLM-Judge, utility) on the same benchmark used for reporting, with a tuned tolerance delta=0.06 on Direct QA. A held-out validation split would make the comparisons more rigorous.

The main results lack variance estimates (no seeds/standard errors), so statements like 'Direct QA changes by ~2-4 points' are hard to judge for statistical significance, particularly for small deltas like UNDIAL's +0.01 on Qwen.

Method novelty is modest: the context term is a standard KL-anchoring device borrowed from RLHF/retention regularization, applied to a new data slice. The paper's value rests more on the diagnostic finding than on the technique, which is acceptable but should be acknowledged more explicitly.

Evaluation is confined to synthetic/fictitious benchmarks (TOFU, PISTOL) and models up to 8B; how the effect manifests on real pretraining-derived knowledge or larger models remains unverified, as the authors themselves note.

The claim that unlearning objectives 'ripple through the representation space' to suppress contextual use is supported mainly by qualitative reasoning in Appendix A.5; mechanistic or ablation evidence for this causal explanation is thin.
